description: How U.S. electricity flipped from coal-dominated grids to a renewables + gas era — 2000–2023
youtube_description:
Title: The US Power Shift — Coal Crushed, Renewables Soar (2000–2023)

Chapters:
0:00 Intro — The big picture (2000 vs 2023)
0:18 2000 Snapshot — Coal dominance (1,953 BkWh)
0:40 The gas surge — Shale gas & gas-fired boom (2005–2016)
1:05 Renewables takeoff — Wind + solar scale up (2010s)
1:30 Nuclear steady — A stable baseline
1:45 COVID & volatility (2020)
2:00 2021–2023 — The new normal and what caused the flip
2:20 Sources & how we built this chart
2:35 Subscribe & follow for more visual histories

Detailed story: This visualization tracks annual U.S. electricity generation by major source from 2000 through 2023 (billions of kWh). In 2000 coal generated roughly 1,953 BkWh — the single-largest source. By 2023 coal plunged to around 690 BkWh (a decline of ~64% from 2000 peak years). Natural gas rose from about 611 BkWh in 2000 to ~1,680 BkWh in 2023 (roughly +175%), driven by the shale gas revolution and new combined-cycle capacity. Renewables (hydro + wind + solar + bio) climbed from ~240 BkWh in 2000 to ~1,250 BkWh in 2023 (+420%), with most growth concentrated after 2010 as wind and solar scaled rapidly. Nuclear remained relatively flat around the ~790 BkWh band across the period.

Why it matters: This is not just a numbers game — it's policy, technology, and economics. Low natural gas prices, EPA regulations, state renewable mandates, and plunging solar/wind costs re-wrote the U.S. generation mix. The result: coal's collapse, gas filling the mid-term balancing role, and renewables emerging as the fastest-growing source.

Sources: U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) annual net generation by source tables; EIA Electric Power Annual; EPA reports on generation mixes. Specific year-by-year figures are from EIA’s state and U.S. totals (2000–2023).

instagram_caption:
🚨 The shock you can see on a chart: coal went from 1,953 BkWh in 2000 to 690 BkWh in 2023 — a collapse of roughly 64% — while renewables exploded from 240 BkWh to 1,250 BkWh (+420%).

Story: In 2000 the U.S. grid was coal-first. Coal supplied nearly half of U.S. electricity (about 1,953 billion kWh) while natural gas generated ~611 billion kWh and renewables were a small slice at ~240 billion kWh. Fast forward: the shale gas revolution, lower gas prices and a policy + cost-driven surge in wind and solar turned the mix on its head. Natural gas climbed to about 1,680 BkWh by 2023 and became the flexible backbone of the grid. Renewables — led by wind and solar — became the fastest-growing source, reaching ~1,250 BkWh in 2023.

Turning points: 2009–2016 marked the gas boom as combined-cycle plants proliferated. The 2010s saw dramatic cost declines in wind and solar; between 2010 and 2023 renewables grew from ~380 BkWh to ~1,250 BkWh — a near quadrupling. Coal’s steep drop accelerated after 2010, with short-term dips (COVID in 2020 drove coal down to ~774 BkWh) and structural declines as older coal plants retired.

Why it matters for you: This is why your utility bill, local air quality, and energy jobs map look different than they did 20 years ago. It’s also why grid operators are scrambling to balance variable renewables with storage and flexible gas capacity.

Question: Which year surprised you the most — the coal collapse, the renewables surge, or the gas boom? Tell me which number jumps out.

facebook_caption:
Headline: The US Power Shift — How Coal Was Dethroned (2000–2023)

Summary: From 2000 to 2023 the U.S. electricity mix underwent a dramatic transformation. Coal generation fell from about 1,953 billion kWh in 2000 to roughly 690 billion kWh in 2023. Natural gas rose from ~611 to ~1,680 billion kWh, and renewables (hydro, wind, solar, bio) expanded from ~240 to ~1,250 billion kWh. Nuclear remained broadly steady near ~790 billion kWh. The shift reflects the combined effects of low gas prices from the shale boom, stricter emissions rules, falling costs for wind and solar, and policy incentives.

This dataset charts year-by-year net generation by major fuel and highlights key inflection points: the gas surge in the late 2000s and early 2010s, renewable scale-up after 2010, and coal retirements through the 2010s and into the 2020s.

Sources: U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) annual generation tables.
